column4: Allah takes responsibility for both جَمْعَهُ, gathering the revelation, and قُرْءَانَهُ, its recitation; this states the section's word-image almost exactly.
Once Allah has recited it, the Prophet is to follow its recitation; the verse distinguishes the divine act of giving the gathered reading from the recipient's faithful following.
The command not to hurry the tongue stages the bodily risk behind the promise of retention: the Prophet need not seize the revelation anxiously before Allah gathers it.
After gathering and recitation in 75:17-18, Allah also assumes its explanation; this completes the passage's account of the divine custody of the delivered words.
The Prophet is told not to hurry the Quran before its revelation is completed; like 87:6, the verse makes reception depend on God's completed delivery rather than anxious self-retention.
Adam forgets a covenant previously entrusted to him, a direct narrative instance of نسي as failing to hold what was deposited with a person.
Pharaoh's question about the القُرُونِ الأُولَى, former generations, supplies the “first/former” side of the answer in 20:52, where their knowledge is retained in writing.
The former generations' knowledge is in a كتاب, and Moses says his Lord neither goes astray nor يَنسَى; writing and the unfailing divine memory coincide exactly as in the section.
A person who forgot the arriving signs is in turn “forgotten”; the reciprocal wording realizes the section's secondary sense of forgetting as deliberate abandonment.
نَسُوا اللَّهَ فَنَسِيَهُمْ explicitly turns human forgetting of God into God's abandonment of them, the very secondary sense used in the source section.
Those who forgot Allah were made to forget themselves, showing forgetting as both an act of abandonment and a divinely imposed loss of what should be held.
The exception “unless Allah wills” is followed by وَاذْكُر رَبَّكَ إِذَا نَسِيتَ; it joins divine willing, forgetting, and remembrance as the recovery from forgetting.
The verse asks whether one was informed of what is in صُحُفِ مُوسَى, directly opening the contents of the Mosaic pages named at 87:19.
Abraham, “the one who fulfilled,” completes the pair of page-bearers named at 87:19 and identifies the second body of earlier scripture whose contents follow.
The first stated teaching of those pages is that no bearer carries another's burden, making the enduring written reminder assign each person an undropped share.
The pages say that a human being has only what he strives for; this specifies the individual portion preserved in the earlier record.
A person's striving will be seen, so the individual share named in 53:39 is not lost from view before recompense.
The striving preserved and shown in 53:39-40 receives its full recompense; this continues the contents of the earlier pages rather than merely standing beside them.
The sequence of teachings from the Mosaic and Abrahamic pages ends by locating the final destination with the Lord, giving the retained teaching its terminus.
The “clear proof” is explicitly connected with what is in الصُّحُفِ الأُولَى, another direct witness that guidance now delivered was already held in the first pages.
The revelation is called a تَذْكِرَة, matching the section's reminder as the means by which a needed thing is brought back to mind.
فَمَن شَاءَ ذَكَرَهُ makes the reminder something a person may actively retain or recall, moving from the instrument in 80:11 to its use.
The reminder of 80:11-12 is located فِي صُحُفٍ مُّكَرَّمَة, explicitly joining recollection to written pages.
The pages are مَرْفُوعَةٍ مُّطَهَّرَة, carrying the surah's height and purification into the physical repository of the reminder.
The passage begins by identifying the Quran as a sending-down from the Lord of the worlds, establishing the divine source of the word later said to be in former books.
The trustworthy Spirit brings the revelation down, making the transmission to the Prophet an entrusted delivery rather than a human compilation.
The revelation descends عَلَىٰ قَلْبِكَ, placing the transmitted words in the heart that must hold them so the Prophet can warn.
The delivered revelation is in a clear Arabic tongue, completing the move from divine descent to articulated, recitable words.
The Quran is said to be in زُبُرِ الأَوَّلِينَ, directly paralleling the section's claim that the recited word is also gathered in earlier scriptures.
Allah says He sent down الذِّكْر and will guard it; the verse unites revelation as Reminder with the divine preservation promised by “you will not forget.”
Gabriel brings the revelation onto the Prophet's heart by Allah's permission while confirming earlier revelation, joining inward retention to continuity across scriptures.
A messenger from Allah يَتْلُو صُحُفًا مُّطَهَّرَة, bringing oral recitation and purified written pages into a single scene.
The purified pages recited in 98:2 contain upright writings, specifying that the physical leaves hold articulated, authoritative content.
The event is made a تَذْكِرَة and a receptive ear “retains it” (تَعِيَهَا أُذُنٌ وَاعِيَة); memory is pictured as a vessel that successfully holds what it receives.
The addressees recite the Book yet “forget yourselves”; the verse exposes a failure to retain and enact the very writing being read.
Israel is told to hold firmly what was given and remember what is in it, directly pairing custody of an entrusted revelation with active remembrance.
The command خُذُوا مَا آتَيْنَاكُم بِقُوَّةٍ وَاذْكُرُوا مَا فِيهِ again makes holding the Book and remembering its contents one act.
A portion of what the covenant people were reminded of was forgotten; this is precisely an entrusted divine communication no longer held intact.
Those who claimed Christianity likewise forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of, a repeated scriptural instance of loss from entrusted memory.
A party given the Book casts Allah's Book behind their backs, turning the section's figurative “dropped” word into an enacted rejection of written revelation.
Those charged to disclose the Book cast it behind their backs and trade it away, showing entrusted writing deliberately abandoned rather than retained and transmitted.
Moses' Book is turned into قَرَاطِيس that people display in part and hide in part; this directly stages earlier revelation as separate written sheets subject to human concealment.
Two travelers forget their fish at the meeting place and it departs into the sea, an unusually exact Quranic scene for the dictionary image of an item left at a travelers' stopping place.
At the rock, the servant recalls that he forgot the fish and even forgot to mention it; a lost object and a lost report are recovered together through recollection.
They turn back عَلَىٰ آثَارِهِمَا, retracing their tracks to seek what escaped; this enacts the section's definition of recollection as “seeking what has gone.”
Allah has enumerated all their deeds while they forgot them (أَحْصَاهُ اللَّهُ وَنَسُوهُ); divine collection preserves exactly what human memory drops.
No leaf falls without Allah knowing it, nothing hidden escapes Him, and all is in a clear Book; falling, hiddenness, knowledge, and written retention meet in one verse.
فَذَكِّرْ بِالْقُرْآنِ مَن يَخَافُ وَعِيدِ closely repeats the command to remind and identifies the receptive hearer as the one who fears.
The command to remind is justified because الذِّكْرَى benefits believers, a direct parallel to 87:9's condition that the reminder be beneficial.
Moses and Aaron are told to address Pharaoh gently so that he may remember or fear; it pairs تذكّر and خشية just as 87:9-10 does.
The effective warning reaches one who follows the Reminder and fears the Merciful unseen, again binding reception of remembrance to fear.
Allah has made the Quran easy for remembrance and asks whether anyone will remember, joining divine facilitation, Quran, and recollection.
The repeated declaration that the Quran is made easy for remembrance reinforces that ease belongs to the divine handling of the recited text.
A third occurrence preserves the same Quran-remembrance formula, making its recurrence itself part of the text's mnemonic design.
The fourth occurrence completes the repeated refrain that the Quran has been made easy for remembrance and awaits a remembering hearer.
Allah says the revelation was made easy “in your tongue” so that they may remember, bringing vocal delivery, ease, and recollection into one formulation.
فَذَكِّرْ إِنَّمَا أَنتَ مُذَكِّرٌ repeats the prophetic stance of 87:9: the Prophet's assigned act is to remind.
The passage asks why they turn away from التَّذْكِرَة, establishing rejected reminder as the problem that the opened pages and divine will later clarify.
Each rejecter demands to be given صُحُفًا مُّنَشَّرَة, separate opened pages, while evading the reminder already before him.
Their demand for pages in 74:52 is diagnosed as a failure to fear the Hereafter, the reverse of the fearing recipient who remembers in 87:10.
The discourse answers the demanded pages by declaring that the existing revelation itself is a تَذْكِرَة.
Whoever wills may remember it, naming the act the reminder-pages are meant to produce.
They will not remember unless Allah wills, directly joining recollection to the same divine-will boundary attached to non-forgetting at 87:7.
The arriving الذِّكْر is immediately identified as a mighty كتاب, explicitly realizing the dictionary sense of Reminder as prophetic book.
Falsehood cannot reach the Book from before or behind; this gives the mighty Reminder of 41:41 a textual inviolability corresponding to divinely secured retention.
The revelation is “only a Reminder and a clear Quran,” placing ذكر and قرآن side by side as two aspects of the same delivered speech.
The object being secured is identified as a glorious Quran, keeping recited revelation in view before its written locus is named.
The glorious Quran is فِي لَوْحٍ مَّحْفُوظٍ, a written tablet explicitly marked as guarded, the clearest counterpart to retained rather than dropped words.
The oath by a “Book inscribed” makes writing itself the object of attention, anticipating the material named in the next verse.
The inscribed Book is on رَقٍّ مَّنشُور, an unrolled parchment, matching the section's lexical definition of a sahifa as material written upon.
The Quran's staged descent strengthens the Prophet's heart and Allah says وَرَتَّلْنَاهُ تَرْتِيلًا; measured joining in recitation serves inward retention.
The Prophet is commanded to recite the Quran with تَرْتِيلًا, the same ordered mode in which the source definition says letters and words are joined.
The Quran is divided so the Prophet may recite it to people deliberately, and it is sent down in stages; collected reading is delivered in an ordered temporal form.
The first command اقْرَأْ gives the section's act of gathering letters into recitation as a divine imperative tied to the Lord's name.
The repeated command اقْرَأْ sustains the act of recitation and attributes its possibility to the generous Lord.
The Lord teaches by the pen, supplying the written counterpart to the repeated oral command to read in 96:1 and 96:3.
God teaches the human being what he did not know, completing the movement from divine teaching through pen to received knowledge.
وَآثَرَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا repeats 87:16's preference for the nearer life almost word for word.
The challenge asks for an earlier كتاب or an أَثَارَةٍ مِّنْ عِلْمٍ; prior writing and a transmitted remnant of knowledge meet in the root family the section connects with reported speech.
Long enjoyment causes a people to forget الذِّكْر, concretely linking preference for passing worldly provision with loss of the enduring reminder.
A companion leads the speaker away from the Reminder after it came to him; the verse stages received guidance being abandoned rather than held.
Satan causes people to forget the remembrance of Allah, making forgetfulness an active displacement of what should occupy and guard memory.
The divine prerogative to abrogate an ayah or cause it to be forgotten marks the explicit boundary around the promise of non-forgetting: any loss is under God's will and replacement.
Allah could, if He willed, take away what He revealed to the Prophet; this identifies the divine-will boundary behind the continued presence of the recited deposit.
Before the Quran the Prophet neither recited a book nor wrote one with his right hand; the verse sharply distinguishes oral reception from human inscription while 29:49 locates the signs inwardly.
If Satan makes the Prophet forget the command to leave mockers, he is to act after recollection; this supplies a bounded, recoverable forgetting alongside 87:6-7's promise.
Those deceived by the worldly life forgot the meeting of their Day, so they are “forgotten”; the verse joins worldly preference to reciprocal abandonment.
Because they forgot the meeting of the Day, they are told “We have forgotten you,” a direct reversal from failed human remembrance to divine abandonment.
The condemned are forgotten as they forgot the meeting of their Day, repeating the deliberate-leaving sense of نسي as retribution.

The hostile claim says the Quran is tales of the former peoples that the Prophet had written down and that are dictated to him; it is a precise counterfeit of the section's divine gathering, recitation, and earlier pages.
The answer to 25:5 says the One who knows the secret in heaven and earth sent it down, restoring divine authorship and hidden knowledge against the scribal accusation.
The magicians refuse to prefer Pharaoh over the clear signs that came to them; their use of نُّؤْثِرَ is the moral reverse of preferring the nearer life over enduring revelation.
“Do not forget your share of the world” sets a boundary around the dunya/Hereafter contrast: worldly participation is retained without making the nearer life the preferred end.
The later state is better than الأُولَى; this reverses preference for the nearer/first condition and uses “first” in a temporal sense beside an enduring better future.
After 5:13-14's forgotten portions, the Messenger exposes much that the People of the Book had hidden; it suggests recovery into disclosure, though concealment is not identical to forgetting.
When a people forget what they were reminded of, their apparent abundance becomes the prelude to sudden seizure; the specific link is reminder received and then lost.
Those who forget what they were reminded of are separated from those who prohibited evil, making retained warning the line between two outcomes.
One reminded of the Lord's signs turns away and forgets what his hands sent ahead; remembrance offered and morally consequential forgetting are directly opposed.
Moses asks not to be blamed for forgetting his undertaking, another narrative case of a condition entrusted to a person but not held; its tie is to ordinary human failure rather than revelation.
Satan makes the released prisoner forget to mention Joseph to his lord; a needed report is not transmitted because it drops from memory.
Mockery of the believers makes the rejecters forget Allah's remembrance, showing attention displaced until the reminder is no longer held.
A second witness is to remind the first if she errs, a concrete legal use of تذكر as retrieving a detail that escaped memory.
“Ask the people of the Reminder” treats custodians of prior revelation as people defined by the retained prophetic book, though the written medium is implicit.
Earlier messengers came with proofs and زُبُر, while the Reminder is sent to the Prophet for explanation; written predecessors and present dhikr are placed in one transmission chain.
The repeated command to ask the people of the Reminder again identifies earlier scriptural knowledge with a community that preserves and can transmit it.
Allah has sent down a كتاب containing the addressees' ذِكْر, explicitly placing remembrance within a revealed book.
Moses and Aaron receive the Criterion, illumination, and a Reminder for the God-fearing, identifying Mosaic revelation with the same dhikr-function as the pages in 87:19.
The present revelation is a blessed Reminder sent down, continuing the prophetic-book sense of ذكر without naming its written form.
Allah says He wrote in the Zabur after the Reminder; the verse links divine writing and prior scripture, though “the Reminder” may denote a heavenly record or an earlier revelation.
Allah relates reports of what has gone before and gives the Prophet a Reminder from Himself, joining transmitted earlier narrative to a present prophetic book.
The revelation is in أُمِّ الْكِتَابِ with Allah, exalted and wise; it provides a heavenly written locus for the recited message.
The Quran is a ذِكْر for the Prophet and his people and they will be questioned about it, treating the revelation as a retained charge as well as remembrance.
The oath by “the Quran possessed of Reminder” joins recited text and الذكر in one compact description, though it does not itself describe the act of preservation.
The Prophet is commanded to recite the revealed Book, whose words none can change; oral delivery is anchored in an inviolable divine text.
In contrast to the absent prior reading or handwriting in 29:48, the revelation is clear signs in the breasts of those given knowledge, an inward repository rather than the Prophet's authored page.
The passage first identifies its object as a noble Quran, keeping recitation before the protected written setting of the next verse.
The noble Quran is “in a guarded/hidden Book,” giving recited revelation a protected written locus; the precise referent is heavenly rather than an ordinary codex.
The guarded Book is approached only by the purified, linking written revelation with purity as 80:13-14 does, though the nature of the touching is interpretively disputed.
The passage closes by naming the Quran as a sending-down from the Lord of the worlds, completing the route from divine source to protected Book.
Even a Book sent down on قِرْطَاس and touched by their hands would be dismissed as magic; the physical sheet clarifies that material presence alone does not secure reception.
The present blessed Book confirms what came before it, completing 6:91's scene of Mosaic sheets with continuity rather than concealment.
Knowledge of the Quran among the scholars of Israel serves as a living sign of the attestation in former books stated in 26:196.
The honored pages are in the hands of سفرة, adding agents who carry or write the repository named in 80:13.
The page-bearers are noble and righteous, completing the scene of an honored, purified, carefully mediated written reminder.
When the صُحُف are spread open, pages become disclosed records at judgment; it is the same physical noun in a different repository from prophetic scripture.
Each person's record is brought out as a كتاب مَّنشُور at resurrection, giving a concrete scene of previously gathered material opened for reading.
“Read your book” transfers the root قرأ to a person's fully gathered record, showing reading as taking together the written account that confronts its owner.
The person given his record says هَاؤُمُ اقْرَءُوا كِتَابِيَهْ, another concrete use of reading a collected written account rather than receiving prophetic recitation.
The judgment Book leaves no small or great deed unenumerated; its exhaustive gathering illuminates the image of nothing entrusted being dropped.
What the earth diminishes from human bodies is known, and with Allah is a حَفِيظ Book; passing material is retained in a preserving record.
No word is uttered without a ready observer, so passing speech is not allowed simply to fall away but is held for record.
Everything the wrongdoers did is in the زُبُر, using the scripture/record noun for gathered deeds rather than prophetic books.
Every small and great thing is inscribed, explaining the completeness of the records named in 54:52.
“Everything We have enumerated in a book” presents writing as the form of exhaustive divine collection.
Nothing hidden in heaven or earth is absent from a clear Book, joining hiddenness to written divine retention as 87:7 joins it to divine knowledge.
The verse moves from the Prophet reciting Quran to God's witnessing and a clear Book from which no particle is absent, specifically connecting recitation with exhaustive record.
Guardians are set over human beings, introducing preservation as active custody before the scribes are named.
The guardians are “noble writers,” giving the custody of 82:10 a scribal mechanism.
The scribes know what people do, completing the movement from known action to guarded writing.
Allah writes what people sent ahead and their آثَار, then enumerates all things in a clear register; “traces” and exhaustive written preservation meet in the root family noted by the section.
The Samiri takes a handful from أَثَرِ الرَّسُول and casts it away; a messenger's trace is physically gathered and then dropped, a pointed reversal of the held transmitted word.
Messengers are sent “upon their traces,” and Jesus is given the Gospel; prophetic succession makes following آثار a vehicle of scriptural transmission.
The hearers know the first creation yet are asked why they do not remember; الأُولَى and تَذَكَّرُونَ join beginning with recollection.
The Hereafter and الأُولَى both belong to Allah, placing the “first” life and the later life under one ownership beside this surah's earlier-page passage.
Allah declares that the Hereafter and الأُولَى belong to Him, setting the same temporal pair against any autonomous preference for the nearer life.
The revelation is a تَذْكِرَة from which whoever wills may take a path to the Lord, presenting reminder as a means for recovering direction.
Human willing in 76:29 operates only if Allah wills, a close structural parallel to the divine-will qualification on retention in 87:7.
The Quran is a Reminder to the worlds, establishing the object whose reception and willing are qualified in the next two ayat.
The Reminder addresses whoever wills to go straight, specifying the responsive agency of its hearer.
The hearers do not will unless Allah wills, placing response to the Reminder within divine willing as 87:7 does with non-forgetting.
“This is a Reminder” followed by the option to take a path to the Lord presents tadhkira as a practical aid, though it does not name memory loss or pages.
The skeptic “forgets his creation”; this may illuminate forgetting one's beginning, which the section associates with الأوّل, but the verse concerns resurrection rather than preservation of words.
